Ongoing studies focus on the optimization of the proposed cutoff algorithm to the clinical settings using a larger patient cohort and thus a larger amount of positive and non-positive lymph nodes. It could be investigated if the algorithm is transferable to y-RGS as well or if it should be redefined for every procedure (i.e., a combination of probe, tracer, and surgical application). Lastly, further optimization of the technique will allow to tailor the amount of injected activity to the given case, thus reducing it further with respect to the current "half PET" starting value. It needs to be highlighted that demonstrating clinical benefit was not in the scope of this initial first-in-human study. However, a recent systematic review on PSMAtargeted surgery [12] indicates that different groups are pursuing different strategies to surgically identity PSMA-positive lesions. To assess the impact of the technology presented in this study, it is critical to compare the sensitivity and specificity to other studies that investigated PSMA-targeted surgery in the primary setting [13, 25-28]. Table 2 indicates that despite the - 3-mmrange tissue penetration of the DROP-IN & radiation, its sensitivity for lymph node detection seems to be at least as good as optimized near-infrared fluorescence guided surgery approaches which are assumed to support a larger signal penetration of <10 mm. This is a rather unique finding, especially when one considers that the B-guidance approach requires about 300 times less of a European Journal of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging (2024) 51:3098-3108 PSMA-targeting tracer and that this can be the exact same tracer already used in the clinic for PSMA-PET. Combined, these features would help reduce costs and stimulate the dissemination of the image guidance concepts to hospitals that have access to [Ga]Ga-PSMA-PET. The performance with B-guidance even equaled some of the y-radioguidance examples, a finding that indicates that limiting the shine-through of background signals with beta detectors could provide a competitive edge. The current study opens up a whole world of possible minimal invasive RGS applications [20]. Firstly, [Ga] Ga-PSMA-guided surgery can be further explored, for example, also in the salvage setting for prostate cancer. There are then nevertheless also other possible options, like FDG-guided surgery (e.g., lung cancer [30]), carbonic anhydrase iX guided surgery (e.g., renal cell carcinoma - ). C-MET guided surgery (e.g., renal cell carcinoma - ), folate guided surgery (e.g., lung cancer [33]), and fibroblast-activation-protein guided surgery (i.e., > 28 different cancer types [34]). To widen the technological impact, the use of 18F-based RGS is being investigated in parallel. Hereby, the results from a study that uses [F]F-FDG in recurrent cervical cancer are encouraging [35]. Applications are expected to improve following technical refinements such as the exploitation of solid-state detectors that are more effective in combination with low-energy positrons as emitted by 18F. with respect to [Ga) [36-38].
